---
title: "Style a Quarto website with CSS and SCSS"
subtitle: "A consistent visual system that helps readers find and understand the work"
---

## Why styling matters

A portfolio should make its purpose and navigation clear before asking the visitor to read technical details. On this site, a deep green establishes the navigation and headings, a warm accent highlights key information, and a neutral background keeps longer explanations readable. The same files style the whole website so individual pages feel connected.

## CSS and SCSS have different roles

**CSS** is the stylesheet language the browser reads. Selectors target HTML elements or classes, and declarations control properties such as spacing, color, and layout. **SCSS** is a Sass syntax that adds features such as variables and nesting. Quarto compiles SCSS into CSS during rendering. A browser does not load SCSS directly.

| File | Role in this portfolio | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `_quarto.yml` | Connect shared theme and styles | `theme: [cosmo, theme.scss]` |
| `theme.scss` | Set Bootstrap variables and reusable rules | `$primary: #164a46;` |
| `styles.css` | Style page components and responsive behavior | `.feature-grid` |

## Connect the theme to the website

The project configuration applies these settings to HTML pages. The dashboard declares the same theme explicitly in its own format settings.

```yaml
format:
  html:
    theme: [cosmo, theme.scss]
    css: styles.css
```

The built-in theme is listed first, followed by the custom SCSS file. In Quarto's theme pipeline, `scss:defaults` provides variables before Bootstrap is compiled, while `scss:rules` adds rules after the theme. This lets me change the palette consistently and then refine specific components. [Quarto's theming documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-themes.html) explains these sections.

## Use SCSS for reusable design choices

This is the actual component rule used by the note below:

```scss
/*-- scss:defaults --*/
$primary: #164a46;
$secondary: #996b38;
$border-radius: .5rem;

/*-- scss:rules --*/
.portfolio-note {
  border-left: 4px solid $secondary;
  padding: 1rem 1.25rem;
  background: mix($secondary, white, 9%);
  border-radius: 0 $border-radius $border-radius 0;
  strong { color: $primary; }
}
```

::: {.portfolio-note}
**Applied example:** This note uses the `.portfolio-note` class. The border calls attention to the message, while the label explains its meaning without relying only on color.
:::

Apply the class in a QMD file with a fenced div:

```markdown
::: {.portfolio-note}
**Applied example:** A message that deserves emphasis.
:::
```

## Use CSS for layout and small-screen behavior

The home page's three skill areas use CSS Grid. On smaller screens they stack vertically instead of squeezing text into narrow columns.

```css
.feature-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
  gap: 1rem;
}
@media (max-width: 760px) {
  .feature-grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
}
a:focus-visible, button:focus-visible, input:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #996b38;
  outline-offset: 4px;
}
```

## The cascade, specificity, and maintainability

When rules conflict, origin, importance, cascade layers, specificity, and source order affect which declaration wins. A class selector such as `.demo-panel` is more specific than an element selector such as `div`; among otherwise equivalent rules, the later one wins. I use component classes and shared variables instead of scattered inline styles or routine `!important` overrides. That makes later changes easier to trace.

::: {.demo-panel}
**A styled component in the rendered page**

This panel demonstrates custom padding, a border, rounded corners, and a heading color. It remains ordinary text that can be selected and read by assistive technology.
:::

## Check the result from the reader's perspective

After changing a style, render the website and review navigation, headings, long text, and the dashboard. Check wide and narrow windows, keyboard focus, descriptive link text, image alternative text, and chart labels. Do not use color as the only indicator of status. Keep the QMD content semantic so the styling improves the reading experience rather than carrying its meaning.
